name: Loratadine
route_note: Oral tablet, orodispersible tablet or syrup once daily

discovery.note: A tricyclic piperidine antihistamine derived from azatadine with little affinity for central H1 receptors.

tagline: Non-sedating antihistamine that became a landmark prescription-to-OTC switch
summary: Loratadine is a long-acting, second-generation H1 antihistamine with minimal sedation at standard doses. It is used for allergic rhinitis and chronic urticaria and is converted in the liver to an active metabolite, desloratadine.
mechanism: Loratadine and desloratadine are inverse agonists at peripheral H1 receptors, blocking histamine-mediated sneezing, rhinorrhoea, itch and wheal formation.
They penetrate the brain poorly, so sedation and anticholinergic effects are uncommon at usual doses.

history.title: US approval
history.detail: FDA approves Claritin as a prescription antihistamine.

history.title: Insurer petition
history.detail: A US health insurer petitions FDA to switch Claritin and other non-sedating antihistamines to OTC status.

history.title: Desloratadine
history.detail: Its active metabolite desloratadine (Clarinex/Aerius) is approved.

history.title: OTC switch
history.detail: Claritin becomes available over the counter in the US, as generics enter.

history.title: Bayer
history.detail: Bayer acquires Merck's consumer care business, including Claritin.

pk.metabolism: Hepatic CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 to desloratadine

facts: The 1998 insurer petition to make Claritin OTC was the first time a third party, not the manufacturer, sought such a switch.
Desloratadine, the active metabolite, was later marketed as a separate drug.
